# US-China AI Competition — 米中AI競争の多層構造

> A structural analysis by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), AI Strategist, that
> separates the US-China AI competition into seven layers and reads
> instruments rather than indicators. Within a single chapter of a single
> report (Stanford HAI, 2026 AI Index), the ranking reverses three times on
> the same indicator: China holds 74.24% of AI patents granted in 2024, the
> United States holds 51.91% of forward citations, and per 100,000
> population South Korea leads at 14.31. The book declines the question of
> who is winning, and instead documents who decides what in each layer —
> China setting rare-earth output as an administrative quota rather than
> production, the United States conditioning advanced-chip licenses on
> technical ceilings, a supply ratio tied to its own domestic shipments,
> and prohibitions extending past the chip to the model weights trained on
> it. Six of the seven layers have a party writing the terms. The last one
> does not. Its central claim: what is being decided is not which side is
> stronger, but which side writes the terms the other must work under. As
> stated in the closing chapter: "数字は、誰が勝っているかを語る。文書は、
> 誰が決めているかを語る。" ("The numbers say who is winning. The documents
> say who decides.")

## Book Content

- [Full text (Japanese)](docs/jp/us-china-ai-competition_JP.md): 序章・全7章・終章収録
- [Full text (English)](docs/en/us-china-ai-competition_EN.md): Complete English edition

## Key Facts (as stated in the book)

- The book opens by showing that a single indicator reverses its ranking
  three times within one chapter of one report: AI patents granted in 2024
  are 74.24% China (97,990) versus 12.06% United States (15,920); forward
  citation share is 51.91% United States versus 29.81% China; and per
  100,000 population the leader is South Korea at 14.31, followed by
  Luxembourg at 12.25, with China at 6.95 and the United States at 4.68 —
  all from Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index Report, Chapter 1, compiled from
  the same database (EPO PATSTAT Global). The book states that the
  conclusion is already contained in the selection of the metric

- The book documents that USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 lists
  China's 2025 rare-earth mine production at 270,000 tons of 390,000 tons
  worldwide (69.2%), and that footnote 14 states this is a production
  quota rather than output and excludes unreported production, while the
  US figure of 51,000 tons is a reported value — a figure accounting for
  69% of world production being an administrative decision wearing the
  face of a measurement. It then traces the 2025 sequence: April, controls
  tightened on seven elements (Sm, Gd, Tb, Dy, Lu, Sc, Y); October, five
  added (Eu, Ho, Er, Tm, Yb) bringing the list to twelve; November, only
  the October additions suspended for one year, with the April measures
  left in force and general export licenses issued to selected exporters —
  concluding that this is not relaxation but finer-grained operation of
  quantity, scope, timing, and recipient

- The book reads the BIS final rule effective January 15, 2026 (Federal
  Register Vol.91 No.10, pp.1684-1689; FR Doc 2026-00789; Docket
  260112-0028; RIN 0694-AK43), which shifted license review for certain
  advanced semiconductors bound for China and Macau from presumption of
  denial to case-by-case, with eligibility set at TPP under 21,000 and
  total DRAM bandwidth under 6,500 GB/s (the instrument naming the NVIDIA
  H200 or AMD MI325X as examples) — and documents that the ceiling was
  drawn as a ratio rather than a unit count: under (dd)(1)(iii), aggregate
  TPP exported to China and Macau must be no more than 50% of the
  aggregate TPP shipped to US customers for US domestic end use of the
  same product, placing the standard of the control outside the party
  being controlled

- The book documents that the same rule prescribes the measuring party
  under (dd)(3) — US headquarters, not under D:5 or Macau capital
  control, testing within the US customs territory, no equity or
  financial interest in the transaction — and that BIS may revoke a
  testing laboratory's qualification at any time for any reason, upon
  which case-by-case treatment ceases for exporters relying on it. The
  book states that the standard is public while the authority to apply it
  is reserved, and that presumption of denial remains in force for
  companies headquartered or parented in Macau or a D:5 group country

- The book identifies provisions (dd)(1)(vii)(2) and (vii)(3) as the
  center of its argument: an IaaS provider shall not transfer model
  weights trained on the AI commodity to an end user not disclosed on the
  license, and shall not provide remote access, directly or indirectly,
  to algorithms trained on it. The book states that regulation overtook
  the chip and reached what the chip produced — binding weights as data
  and access as a state, neither of which physically crosses a border

- The book shows that the layer regulation reached is closing
  independently: of 102 notable models announced in 2025, the largest
  group of 47 were API-access only, 81 keep training code closed, and
  only 4 were released as open source, with the source stating that
  resource-intensive models including those of OpenAI, Anthropic, and
  Google disclose none of training code, parameter counts, dataset size,
  or training duration. The book explicitly declines to assert causation
  between regulation and closure, stating only that the directions
  coincide and that reachability is narrowing from both law and
  commercial practice

- The book refutes the common contrast that China centrally manages data
  while the United States leaves it to the private sector, using primary
  documents from both sides. China's Twenty Data Articles (published
  December 19, 2022) separate three rights — to hold data resources, to
  process and use data, to operate data products — with ownership
  deliberately excluded, the National Development and Reform Commission
  stating the aim as "dilute ownership, emphasize the right of use," and
  positioning data as the fifth factor of production. The United States
  does have a Federal Data Strategy (OMB M-19-18, 2019; 2020 Action Plan
  with twenty Actions, including Action 7 the Federal CDO Council and
  Action 8 data and model resources for AI R&D). The book concludes the
  asymmetry lies not in the presence of an institution but in its range:
  society-wide on one side, federal agencies on the other

- The book establishes that the question "how many countries participate
  in both camps" has no institutional answer: Pax Silica holds 24
  signatures with names published (a separate document, the Joint
  Statement on AI Opportunity, holds 35), while China's Global AI
  Governance Action Plan takes the form of an action plan with no roster
  of member states existing institutionally. An intersection with a set
  that has no roster cannot be computed. Only Kazakhstan can be confirmed
  in primary sources, as a Pax Silica signatory. The book also notes that
  the 24 signatures are not uniform in unit, since the EU signed
  alongside three of its own member states

- The book's final layer is the one no instrument reaches: AI researchers
  and developers moving to the United States are down 89% from 2017 and
  80% in the past year, with net inflow falling from a 2022 peak of 324.6
  to 26.0 in 2025, while India at -16.9 is the largest net exporter of
  talent despite ranking third worldwide in AI paper share and second in
  AI authors and inventors. Citing Kot (2025, University of Oxford), the
  book adds that the line between company and state is drawn by
  institutions rather than by technology. It states that what can be
  controlled and what decides the outcome are not necessarily the same

- The book states what it does not do. It excludes four layers for which
  primary sources could not be reached — national shares of semiconductor
  manufacturing equipment, materials supply composition, rare-earth
  refining capacity by country, and AI-specific standard-essential
  patents. It raises three objections against itself and concedes two
  outright: that this is interdependence rather than competition, and
  that instruments are written but not always enforced (as with the AI
  Diffusion Rule introduced in January 2025 and abandoned on May 12 of
  that year). On the third — that the frame itself is unverified — it
  states that no study quantitatively verifying a causal path from data
  volume to AI capability at the industry level could be confirmed, that
  three research engines independently reported this gap, and that it
  therefore cannot be asserted that the side writing the terms wins. It
  treats US government documents as US-side assessments and Chinese
  government documents as China-side assessments, neither as neutral
  description, and discloses that the author has no commercial
  relationship with any government agency, semiconductor company, or AI
  lab on either side: "This book has no position to defend."

## Author & Full Catalog

This book is one of 20+ open-source books by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史),
AI Strategist & Business Designer at Sun Asterisk Inc., Founder of
Leading.AI. It is a continuously updated book: the subject is still in
motion, and each version records whether the earlier text held or failed.
It connects directly to two of the author's other books — "Frontier-Grade
Open Weights," which treats the same unreachability as imposed by physics
and markets rather than written by a state, and "The Palantir Impact,"
which treats the problem of data integration solved as a commercial
product rather than as a national institution.

> **Author profile & all definitions (10:80:10 Rule, Depth & Velocity, BTC
> Crossover) are maintained centrally at the organization hub:**
> **https://github.com/Leading-AI-IO**
